analysis.one_liner: Requires the Supreme Court to adopt and publish a code of conduct and process misconduct complaints.
analysis.headline: The Supreme Court Code of Conduct Act was introduced with one cosponsor, never received a committee vote or floor action, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Supreme Court to write a code of conduct for its nine justices within a year, publish it on the Court's website, and designate someone to receive and process complaints alleging that a justice broke federal law or the code. A designated officer would publish an annual report of complaints, with complainants' names removed, and could bring in federal investigators to look into alleged misconduct. Today the Supreme Court is the only federal court whose judges are not formally bound by an enforced code of conduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Members of the public who file complaints about justices' conduct, and anyone relying on the Court's impartiality, because complaints would be documented publicly and published in an annual report rather than disappearing without record.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens filing complaints against justices

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Court to issue, after public notice and comment, a code of conduct covering the Chief Justice and the associate justices, and publish it on the Court's website [S3].

Requires the Court to designate an individual to process complaints alleging that a justice engaged in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice or in violation of federal law or the code [S3].
Requires the designated individual to publish an annual report describing the complaints received, with complainants' names anonymized, and any steps taken to remedy the conduct [S3].
Allows the Marshal of the Supreme Court to bring in federal investigative personnel or government contractors to help investigate alleged misconduct by justices or their employees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The nine justices, who would lose the ability to police their own conduct privately and would be subject to documented complaints and published reporting for the first time. The cost to taxpayers is minimal.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement stays largely inside the Court: the complaint designee is chosen by the Court itself, investigations run through the Marshal after consultation with the Chief Justice, and the bill sets no penalty for a justice who violates the code [S3].

The bill addresses written complaints and publication, but it does not change recusal decisions, so a justice who declines to step aside from a case would face no formal consequence under this bill [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a real but modest step: it would end the Supreme Court's status as the only federal court without a public code of conduct and create a paper trail of complaints. Its weakness is that it trusts the Court to police itself, since the Court picks the complaint processor and sets no penalties. The cost to the public is negligible; the main loss falls on justices who would lose unrecorded discretion.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late April 2023 and read twice, the bill went to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without a single committee vote or floor action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 26, 2023 by Senator Angus King and referred the same day to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S5].
Its only cosponsor was Senator Lisa Murkowski, one Republican, and no other senators signed on over the life of the bill [S4].
No markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the action history ends with the referral to Judiciary [S5].
The bill's death meant the justices continued to operate without a congressional requirement to adopt or publish a code of conduct or to process misconduct complaints [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nine Supreme Court justices are better off: no code of conduct or public complaint process was imposed on them, and the Court remained the only federal court exempt from an enforced ethics code.

for.name: Sen. Angus King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Supreme Court Code of Conduct Act and sent it to the Senate Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it its only Republican support.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split was recorded; the bill's support was one independent sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, and no Democratic senators publicly signed on.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the justices' position as the only federal judges not bound by a published, complaint-driven code of conduct, exposing complaints about their conduct to public reporting. Their interest in keeping conduct matters private ran against the public's interest in a documented accountability process.
